summary: The study investigates the use of zinc oxide (ZnO) grown by atomic layer deposition (ALD) for 3D electronics, particularly cross-bar memories. The material is grown at low temperatures (100–300 8C) using diethylzinc and deionized water as precursors. The electrical properties of ZnO-ALD films, such as electron mobility and free carrier concentration, are evaluated for their suitability in 3D electronic devices. Monocrystalline ZnO films grown at 250 8C and above show high electron mobility (up to 174 cm²/Vs) and free carrier concentration (around 3.9 × 10¹⁸ cm⁻³), while polycrystalline films grown at lower temperatures (100 8C) have lower mobility but suitable carrier concentration for Schottky junction applications. The study highlights the potential of ZnO-ALD films for low-temperature 3D electronics.
evidence: We demonstrate that electrical parameters of ZnO grown by the atomic layer deposition (ALD) method at low temperature limit (100–200 8C) fulfill requirements for 3D electronic devices, because electron carrier mobility is above 10 cm²/Vs and n concentration at the level of 1 /C² 10¹⁷ cm/C0 3. In this paper we report on electrical, optical, and structural properties of zinc oxide grown by the atomic layer deposition (ALD) technique at temperature of 300 8C and below. We show that physical properties of ZnO-ALD thin films make this material a prospective candidate for a novel application in 3D electronics, especially for cross-bar memories. The study also discusses the use of diethylzinc (DEZn) and deionized water as precursors for ZnO growth by ALD.
